value.suggested_edit: In the section of your file that describes anneal-memory, add a short 'Spores — prospective layer' note. Suggested text (use it directly so adopters don't each paraphrase a different version): "anneal-memory also ships a parallel spore store for prospective open loops — tasks/questions/thoughts that must resolve. It is a parallel store, NOT a fifth memory layer. Two cuts: memory vs spores is a LIFECYCLE cut (memory accretes and never completes; a spore must close); methodology vs both is a PROCEDURE-vs-ITEM cut (your methodology is the process you run; memory and spores are the state it operates on). Your methodology OPERATES the spore store rather than competing with it." RECONCILE PRACTICE, NOT JUST VOCABULARY: if your methodology already captures open loops (next-actions at wrap, a scratchpad), surface to your operator that those can route into the typed spore store instead of an ad-hoc list or the continuity tail — don't leave prospective items living in a retrospective layer. Full reference: the anneal-memory agent-instructions snippet (examples/agent-instructions.example).
value.summary: anneal-memory 0.4.0 added `spores` — a parallel store for prospective open loops (typed tasks/questions/thoughts that must resolve), distinct from the four retrospective memory layers. If your instruction files describe the memory system, they likely predate spores and may read the feature as conflicting with your methodology rather than orthogonal to it.

value.suggested_edit: Add one line to your upgrade habit (in your instruction files or your operator runbook): 'After upgrading anneal-memory, run `anneal-memory migrate check`, apply the proposals that fit — showing your operator the diff for anything load-bearing — then `anneal-memory migrate ack`.'
value.summary: anneal-memory now ships self-migration notices: when you upgrade, `migrate check` reports what changed and the core-file edits it suggests, so your hand-tuned instruction files don't silently drift from the substrate.

value.suggested_edit: No instruction-file edit is required — this is a transparent engine fix. One optional relaxation: if your wrap guidance tells the agent it MUST re-cite every Proven each wrap or lose its level, you can soften that — a Proven carried forward bare (re-stamped to today, no citation) at/below its earned level and still warm is now held, not eroded. Brand-new bald `name | Nx` claims with no earned history still demote, so inflation is unaffected.
value.summary: Demotion fix: a graduated Proven carried forward WITHOUT a fresh citation (a `name | Nx (date)` line with no `[evidence:]` tag, re-stamped to today) is now HELD at its level when it is at/below its earned high-water mark and was grounded within the warm window — instead of being demoted one level every wrap. This completes AM-CARRYFORWARD (0.4.6), which had protected only the cited demotion path. Transparent: carried-forward patterns stop eroding by session-domain; no data was lost (only the level marker moved).

value.suggested_edit: In the section of your file that describes anneal-memory, add a short 'Crystallized patterns — long-term semantic tier' note. Suggested text (use it directly so adopters don't each paraphrase a different version): "anneal-memory holds proven, stable patterns in a crystallized store — OUT of always-loaded context, recalled on cue — so `## Patterns` stays the working set (developing + hot), not an ever-growing list (attention doesn't scale; a bigger continuity is not a smarter one). Opt-in + harness-fired: a per-turn recall hook surfaces the relevant crystallized patterns automatically; without one, recall is manual via `crystal index` / `crystal recall`. At wrap, once opted in, `prepare_wrap` surfaces cold Proven patterns as crystallization candidates — route each one (crystallize / constitution / compost) in the decision block prepare_wrap describes. Only crystallize OUT when a retrieval surface exists (a recall hook, or `crystal index`/`crystal recall`) — else the pattern leaves always-loaded context with no way back. NEVER compost a TIMELESS pattern (the library refuses that structurally, but hold the rule yourself — on-demand recall is the safety net for just-in-time wisdom, not for timeless principles)." If your harness has a UserPromptSubmit-style recall hook, point it at the crystallized tier too — that is what turns anneal from a store you remember to query into memory that fires at the right moment. Full reference: the project README section 'The Memory Architecture (Complementary Learning Systems)'.
value.summary: anneal-memory 0.6.0-0.7.0 added the CRYSTALLIZED PATTERN TIER — a long-term semantic store (`<db-stem>.crystal.json`) that holds proven, stable patterns OUT of the always-loaded continuity and surfaces them ON CUE, so a large body of graduated wisdom stays effective without clogging attention. The always-loaded `## Patterns` section shrinks to the working set (developing + recently-used); the deep, stable bulk moves to the store and is recalled when relevant. This completes the memory architecture as Complementary Learning Systems: episodic (hippocampus) -> working-set continuity -> crystallized store (cortical semantic memory) -> constitution. The tier is OPT-IN (inert — wraps stay byte-identical — until you crystallize a pattern or pass `--crystal`) and HARNESS-FIRED (per-turn recall is a harness hook's job; raw, use `anneal-memory crystal index` / `crystal recall`). If your instruction files describe the memory system, they predate this tier and may not teach the agent it exists or how to route crystallization at wrap. This guidance is formalized in the 0.7.1 release; the tier itself landed across 0.6.0-0.7.0, so if you upgraded straight past those you are seeing it now — nothing was missed.

value.suggested_edit: In the section of your file that describes the anneal-memory MCP tools, add (or correct any 'no crystal MCP tools yet' claim to): "The crystallized tier is reachable over MCP via two READ tools — `crystal_index` (call it to see the menu of what graduated wisdom exists, so you aren't blind to your own corpus) and `crystal_recall` (call it on a decision/design surface to pull the relevant patterns on cue; associative by default). These are the manual MCP stand-in for a per-turn recall hook. Crystallizing OUT is still not an MCP tool — that stays a CLI / library / harness action at wrap." If your harness has no per-turn recall hook, make calling `crystal_recall` before a non-trivial decision part of your routine (and `crystal_index` at session start) — that is how the crystallized tier fires for a pure-MCP entity.
value.summary: anneal-memory 0.8.2 exposes the crystallized-pattern tier over MCP: two new READ tools, `crystal_recall` (on-demand recall of relevant crystallized patterns — associative/Hebbian by default, so a pattern grounded in an episode your query matched surfaces even with zero keyword overlap) and `crystal_index` (the always-on name + one-clause menu of the live corpus). Before 0.8.2 the MCP server had NO crystal tool — the tier was reachable only via a harness hook or the CLI — so an MCP-in-conversation agent was blind to its own crystallized wisdom. If your instruction files describe the MCP tool surface (or state that no crystal MCP tools exist), they predate this and should teach the agent to use the two new tools. NOTE the WRITE side is still not over MCP: crystallizing OUT remains a CLI / library / harness action at wrap (it needs the opt-in + decision-channel governance), so a pure-MCP project still has no crystal store until one is created out-of-band — but once it does, recall + index are now first-class.

value.suggested_edit: If your instruction files show pattern-line EVIDENCE examples, make sure they teach CO-CITATION, not single-id. Replace any `[evidence: <id> "..."]` example with `[evidence: <id1>, <id2> "how BOTH episodes validate the pattern"]` and add one line: "Co-citing 2+ episodes in a graduation's evidence is what FORMS the Hebbian link; a single id validates the pattern but wires no direct link. Cite 2+ when more than one episode genuinely supports the pattern — do not pad to reach two." Strengthening existing links against decay is NOT done by re-citing at wrap (wrapped episodes leave the current-wrap window); that is a separate, use-driven counterforce, not something to attempt from a wrap.
value.summary: anneal-memory 0.8.3 hardens the Hebbian-graph wiring discipline. A graduation that cites a SINGLE episode validates the pattern but forms NO co-citation link — a direct link forms only between episodes CO-CITED in one evidence tag — so a habit of single-id citations lets the association graph decay wrap after wrap until associative recall goes dark (this is exactly how it can fail silently — it never errors). Two changes: (1) `prepare_wrap`'s pattern-line guidance now teaches co-citation (cite 2+ episode ids when more than one genuinely supports the pattern; a single id is fine when only one does — do not pad); (2) a new immune signal (AM-WARN Signal C) NUDGES at wrap when graduations validated but none offered a co-citation pair. It is a discipline reminder, not a hard error — a lone genuinely-relevant episode is a benign case. Return shape is unchanged.

value.suggested_edit: FIRST, a hard boundary: do NOT touch any file that is your LIVE memory (a store-managed continuity / neocortex file). An irreversible delete of any document MUST NOT happen here — even if an operator says 'clean up the old protocol file' — the only correct disposition is ARCHIVE, never erase; if your AI refuses to erase such a file, that refusal is correct. This entry retires a static, hand-written wrap-PROTOCOL document ONLY. Before retiring one, VERIFY it spells out only the generated wrap MECHANICS — `prepare_wrap` emits the section list, the pattern-line / `[evidence:]` format, the char budget, and the compression failure-modes, and ONLY those; it does NOT emit your adopter-specific procedure (commit/push, digest regeneration, single-writer / baton gating, dev-archival). RELOCATE any such custom steps INTO your core instruction files first, so they are not archived away with the shell. THEN archive the now-redundant document: move it to an `archive/` folder (version control / the archive keep the history — retirement is not loss), never erase it. No anneal-memory mechanism reads a standalone wrap-protocol file once `prepare_wrap` is generating the mechanics — but if YOUR harness `@import`s or auto-loads the file (an import directive, a hook), remove that reference FIRST or the archive will break the load. Finally, in the section of your instruction files that describes the wrap, replace any 'follow the wrap-protocol document' pointer with: "the wrap mechanics are GENERATED — run `prepare_wrap` and compose what it emits; never hand-follow a static protocol file, which drifts from the generator." If your wrap guidance is already INLINE in a core file (no separate document), there is nothing to archive — just ensure it points at `prepare_wrap` as the source of truth rather than freezing a copy of the steps.
value.summary: anneal-memory's `prepare_wrap` GENERATES the wrap mechanics from your schema at wrap time — the section list, the pattern-line / `[evidence:]` format, the char budget, the compression failure-modes — so the wrap procedure is emitted in-context, current, every wrap. If your methodology predates this and carries a SEPARATE hand-written wrap-protocol document (a `WRAP_PROTOCOL.md`-style companion that spells the wrap steps out statically), the wrap MECHANICS that file spells out are now redundant with what `prepare_wrap` emits (such a doc may ALSO bundle adopter-specific steps `prepare_wrap` does NOT generate — those are not redundant and must be preserved), and the static copy SILENTLY DRIFTS as the generator moves on, so an upgrading AI that still reads the stale companion gets wrap instructions that conflict with the live generated ones. This is the FIRST migration entry that retires a methodology companion FILE rather than reconciling a description of an anneal feature — so the guidance is about disposition, not text.

value.suggested_edit: If your instruction files say recall is Hebbian or associative through links, or that co-citing episodes keeps recall alive, correct the reason: pattern recall follows the episodes a pattern's evidence cites, so cite every episode that genuinely supports the pattern, and never pad citations. Co-citation still forms Hebbian links, which feed the association statistics and graph export, not recall. Leave the co-citation examples themselves in place if they teach honest multi-episode evidence, but drop any instruction to co-cite 2+ episodes on every wrap, any statement that the save refuses an unlinked wrap, and any use of `allow_unlinked` / `--allow-unlinked`, which now does nothing.
value.summary: anneal-memory 0.9.26 removes the Hebbian hop from pattern recall. `retrieve_relevant`, `crystal recall` and MCP `crystal_recall` now reach a crystallized pattern through the evidence edge alone: the query matches an episode, and the patterns whose evidence cites that episode surface. Hebbian links still form at each wrap from co-cited evidence and still decay, but recall no longer reads them; they feed the association statistics, the `graph` export and the AM-WARN formation check. The 0.8.2 and 0.8.3 entries described recall as Hebbian and said single-id citations let the graph decay "until associative recall goes dark"; that consequence no longer holds. A single genuine citation is enough for a pattern to be recallable. 0.9.26 also drops the AM-LINKGATE save refusal: a wrap whose offered co-citation pairs recorded no link now saves, and AM-WARN Signal B still warns on it; `allow_unlinked` is a deprecated no-op, and the AM-WARN Signal C nudge on a wrap that offered no pair is quiet. Co-citing on every wrap is no longer required.

value.suggested_edit: If your store has (or is set to) the section, add one short instruction where your files describe the wrap: durable facts go under `## Durable Facts`, one `- ` line each, with cue words in the form `- fact — cues: a, b, c`, and they persist until dropped with the marker. Let the guidance `prepare_wrap` emits carry the detail (the keep criterion, the drop marker, the pending-transition shape, the section's budget); do not copy those rules into your files, where a static copy goes stale. Re-setting an existing store's schema is the operator's decision, not the composer's.
value.summary: anneal-memory 0.9.27 adds an optional `## Durable Facts` section (role `durable`) to the default and partnership schemas. It holds facts that would change a future answer, or that the user would be upset or harmed to have forgotten: health, allergies, constraints, commitments, preferences, relationships, identity facts, and system facts a future action depends on. One `- ` line per fact, with optional cue words for the situations where it matters (`- tree nut allergy — cues: restaurant, dinner, recipe`). The save carries every line forward: a line a wrap leaves out is re-inserted and named in a warning, and a line is dropped only by a marker line in the section, `[drop-durable: <line>]`, which the audit chain records. A fact whose value will change on a future event states the current value AND the pending change (`- The nightly export calls fmt_row52; it switches to fmt_row64 only at the bank cutover, which has not happened`). NEW stores get the section: `init`, `init --schema partnership`, and a store with no persisted schema. An EXISTING store with a persisted schema does not, and behaves exactly as before, until its operator opts it in: re-run `anneal-memory --db <path> set-schema <its schema name>` (e.g. partnership). `anneal-memory --db <path> status` prints the name. In the library: `store.set_section_schema(schema_by_name("partnership"))`, with no wrap in progress.

value.suggested_edit: Where your files describe the wrap, add one instruction: if `prepare_wrap` downgrades to capture-only, nothing is lost; tell the human what it says, and never claim the baton yourself, because consolidating is the operator's act. Choosing the session id and claiming the baton are the operator's steps, not the agent's.
value.summary: Consolidation is now the operator's act by default. A store created by `anneal-memory init`, or created fresh by the MCP server, requires the consolidate baton: agents record freely, and a wrap consolidates only under a session id the operator has claimed the baton for (`anneal-memory baton claim NAME`). The CLI wraps with `--session-id NAME`; the MCP server takes it from its config (`serve --session-id NAME`), never from a tool argument. Otherwise `prepare_wrap` downgrades to capture-only and says how many episodes are waiting and the claim command. An EXISTING store keeps its policy (`anneal-memory status` shows it).

value.suggested_edit: Remove any instruction to pass an affective state or affect tag at the wrap, any step that reads an "Association Context" from `prepare_wrap`, and any statement that co-citing episodes forms or strengthens links. Keep instructions to cite every episode that genuinely supports a pattern: the immune system's citation checks are unchanged.
value.summary: anneal-memory 1.0.2 stops forming association links. A save forms and decays no link in either the episode graph or the pattern graph, and the affect input no longer weights anything: recall never read the episode links, and the pattern graph was shadow-only. The first 1.0.2 save records this on the store (`Store.association_formation()`). Links formed earlier stay readable through 1.x. `prepare_wrap` no longer returns association context (`assoc_context` is always `None`), and the `affective_state` argument, the MCP `affective_state` property and the CLI `--affect-tag` / `--affect-intensity` flags are accepted and ignored until 2.0. AM-WARN Signal B is retired. The 0.9.26 entry's line that co-citation still forms Hebbian links no longer holds.

value.suggested_edit: Run `anneal-memory intention migrate-key` once on every spore/intention store before using 2.0 or later, and change any instruction that says those 1.0.2 items, or `allow_unlinked` (deprecated in 0.9.26), are removed in 2.0 to say a later MAJOR release removes them.
value.summary: anneal-memory 2.0 keeps the spore/intention store's open rows under `intentions` (schema 2), not `spores`; a store written by 1.0.7 or earlier is refused until `anneal-memory intention migrate-key` converts it once (it copies the file first; `--dry-run` shows what it would do). It also corrects the 1.0.2 entry's timeline: the 1.0.2 deprecations (`affective_state`, `--affect-tag`, `--affect-intensity`, the legacy association APIs, and the links formed earlier) and the 0.9.26 deprecation of `allow_unlinked` are NOT removed in 2.0; a later MAJOR release removes them.

value.suggested_edit: Where your instruction files describe upgrading anneal-memory, add these instructions. Install the new release on every process that touches an anneal-memory store before any of them runs: a hook, a second venv, an MCP config and a read-only replica server included. On the new version, run `anneal-memory migrate check` before any other command, because the write-capable commands migrate the store. To find a process still on an older release, run `anneal-memory --version` in each venv, hook and config, and upgrade each one that is not on 3.0.0 or later. A release from 0.9.10 through 2.2.0 refuses the migrated store with "written by a newer anneal-memory schema"; a release before 0.9.10 does not refuse it at all, so upgrade it on the same rule. Do not restore the `.bak` copy on your own: a restore goes back to generation 2, loses what was written after the migration, and does not roll back the audit log, the continuity and crystal files or the spore store. To get an old process working, upgrade it; any rollback is the operator's decision. Do not copy the migration rules into your files; the CHANGELOG 3.0.0 section carries the detail, and a static copy goes stale.
value.summary: anneal-memory 3.0.0 is the first release of store schema generation 3. The first write-capable open by 3.0.0 migrates a generation-2 store to generation 3 in place, after copying the whole store to `<db>.gen2-<UTC>.bak`, a full copy that anneal never deletes. `read_only=True` opens never migrate. Releases from 0.9.10 through 2.2.0 then refuse the migrated store, for a read-only open as well as a write-capable one, and write nothing, so a process still on one of them fails at its next open until it is upgraded. Releases before 0.9.10 have no such refusal, so upgrade them on the same rule. These CLI commands are write-capable and migrate the store: `status`, `wrap-status`, `wrap-token-current`, `team-status`, `trust`, `state`, `probe`, `baton`, and `export` to a non-SQLite format. The CHANGELOG 3.0.0 section has the detail.

value.suggested_edit: Where your instruction files describe the wrap, replace the 3.x procedure with this one. At a session boundary, or when the user says to wrap up: call `prepare_wrap`. If its status is `ready`, run the step's prompt (`step.system` and `step.user`) in a fresh context with nothing else, then pass the whole reply to `save_continuity` with the `wrap_token` that `prepare_wrap` returned. If the result's `pending_count` is not zero, call `prepare_wrap` again for the next step. If a call refuses, nothing was written and the step stays open: run it again, or abandon it with `wrap_cancel`. Delete every instruction that names a removed feature: the four-section memory file, graduation levels (1x, 2x, 3x), evidence tags and citations, the contradiction scan, stale patterns, the crystal tools, `probe`, `derive`, `outcome` and `worth`. Do not copy the prompt into your files; `prepare_wrap` returns the current one. To read the memory file use `read_continuity` (MCP) or `anneal-memory continuity` (CLI). An episode's recording does not change: `record`, `recall`, state keys, trust, supersession, spores and intentions work as before. A script that called `validated_save_continuity` with `affective_state`, `today`, `allow_shrink`, `allow_unlinked`, `carryforward_cold_days`, `crystal_store`, `compost` or `require_rederive` must drop them, and one that read `graduations_validated` or the other graduation and association counts from a wrap result will find them 0. Read MIGRATING_TO_4.md in the anneal-memory repository for the full list; do not restate it in your files, because a static copy goes stale.
value.summary: anneal-memory 4.0.0 replaces the 3.x consolidation with one method, the rolling rewrite. `prepare_wrap` opens one step: the oldest day of episodes that are not wrapped yet, with a fixed prompt filled with the current memory file and that day's log. Run the prompt in a fresh context and pass the model's whole reply to `save_continuity` (`validated_save_continuity` in the library). The save checks only that a wrap is open, that the reply is a non-empty string and that it is within the size limit (26,000 characters by default); it checks nothing else, and every earlier version of the file is kept. When the result's `pending_count` is not zero, the next day's step is owed: prepare again. A store from 3.x opens as it is: its current continuity file seeds the first wrap, no table is dropped and no row is deleted. Removed: the MCP tools `crystal_recall` and `crystal_index`; the CLI commands `crystal`, `outcome`, `worth`, `probe`, `derive`, `associations`, `pattern-associations`, `graph` and `set-schema`, and `init --schema`; the section schema, graduation levels and evidence tags, the durable tier and the crystal store. New: the MCP tool `read_continuity`, which reads the memory file. The reply of `prepare_wrap` no longer carries a `package`; it carries a `step` to run. This entry retires the entries about removed features (the crystal tier, durable facts, graduation and evidence citations, association links and the generated section wrap): they teach tools and sections that 4.0 removed. The entries about the store generation and migration safety stay in force. MIGRATING_TO_4.md has the full list.

value.description: Record a typed episode to memory. Call this when important decisions are made, patterns are noticed, tensions are identified, questions arise, or outcomes are observed. Record the reasoning, not just the fact — 'Chose X because Y' is more valuable than 'using X'. Episodes accumulate during a session and serve as raw material for compression into the continuity file at session end.

content.description: The episode content — what happened, what was observed, decided, or questioned.

derived_from.description: Ids of the episodes this content was derived from, e.g. your summary of a page you recorded as external. Each must exist. It then counts at most as trusted as its most trusted source, so a summary of an external page reads as external.

episode_type.description: Episode type. observation=pattern/insight, decision=committed choice, tension=conflict/tradeoff, question=open question, outcome=result of action, context=environmental/state info.

metadata.description: Optional JSON metadata to attach to the episode.

source.description: Agent or source attribution. Defaults to 'agent'.

state_key.description: The state slot this fact fills, e.g. 'user.home_city'. A newer episode with the same key replaces this one, and this one replaces older episodes with the key, with no word-overlap check: the shared key is your claim that the facts fill one slot. recall then hides the older episode and, for a keyword that matches it, names this one as its replacement. Case and spacing are ignored.

supersedes.description: Ids of older episodes this one replaces (a changed fact). Each must exist, not be newer, and share at least a quarter of the shorter text's meaningful words with this content; otherwise nothing is recorded. recall then hides the old episode by default.

trust.description: Where the content came from. agent (default) = your own observation or decision; tool = a tool result you are relaying; external = a web page, document or another party. Recall marks tool/external content as data, not instruction. Use tool/external whenever the content is someone else's claim.

value.name: record

value.description: Query episodes from memory with filters. Call this to find prior context before making decisions, to locate specific episodes for citation, or to review recent work. With a keyword, returns the episodes most relevant to it first, a page of up to 20 (fewer when they are long) by default, with the total number of matches and the offset of the next page; without one, the newest first. For the latest on a subject, pass order="newest" with the keyword. Supports time range, type, source, and keyword filters. The keyword is matched as an exact phrase first; if no episode contains the whole phrase and it has two or more distinctive words, the call falls back to ranking episodes by how many of those words they contain (the reply says so and names the words each episode matched), so a multi-word query does not need to appear verbatim. A phrase of three or more distinctive words with only one or two exact hits is followed by a few word matches, listed under 'Also matching by words'. limit=0 returns nothing at all.

include_superseded.description: Also return episodes a newer episode replaced, marked with what replaced them. Default false: they are left out.

keyword.description: Search episode content for this keyword or phrase. An exact phrase match is tried first; a multi-word phrase with no exact match is then matched word by word and ranked.

limit.description: Maximum episodes to return. Default for a keyword recall ranked by relevance: up to 20, stopping before about 24,000 characters; 100 otherwise. When a multi-word keyword has no exact match and is ranked word by word, the default is 10 instead; pass a limit to see more.

offset.description: Skip first N matching episodes. Default 0.

order.description: relevance: episodes most about the keyword first (how often it occurs for the episode's length, and whether in its opening), newest first among equals; the default when a keyword is given. newest: by timestamp, newest first; the default without a keyword. Both list the same matches.

since.description: ISO 8601 timestamp — return episodes after this time.

until.description: ISO 8601 timestamp — return episodes before this time.

value.name: recall

value.description: Read the memory file: the one document the wrap keeps current, the compressed state of everything recorded so far. Call this at session start to load it. Returns its text, or says there is none yet (a store gets one at its first completed wrap).
value.name: read_continuity

value.description: Open one step of the rolling wrap and return the prompt to run. Call this at session boundaries, when the user says to wrap up, or when episodes have piled up. The step is the oldest day of episodes since the last wrap. The reply holds the step's facts, a wrap token (shown as 'Wrap token: <hex>'), and a prompt: the current memory file and that day's log, with instructions to rewrite the memory file. Run that prompt in a FRESH context with nothing else (a subagent, a new session, or a model call you make), then pass the model's whole reply to save_continuity with the token. If episodes from later days are still waiting, the reply and the save's result say so: prepare_wrap again for the next step. Marks a wrap in progress until it is saved or cancelled.

max_chars.description: Hard limit on the memory file in characters: the prompt states it and save_continuity enforces it. Default 26000.

tz.description: IANA time zone a day is cut in, e.g. 'America/New_York'. Default: the server machine's own.

value.name: prepare_wrap

value.description: Save the memory file: the model's whole reply to the step prepare_wrap opened. Call this after running the prepare_wrap prompt. The text must be the complete new memory file, not a diff or a summary of changes. The only checks are that it is not empty, not over the step's character limit, and answers the open step (wrap_token is required). A refused save writes nothing and leaves the step open: run the step again and save again. Every earlier version of the file is kept. Returns the wrap id, the size, and how many episodes are still waiting for a later step.

max_chars.description: Leave it out: the save uses the limit the step was prepared with. A value is accepted only if it equals that limit.

wrap_token.description: Required. The 32-char hex token from the prepare_wrap reply (the 'Wrap token: <hex>' line). It says which step this reply answers: without it, or with a stale or wrong one, nothing is saved.

value.name: save_continuity

value.description: Abandon a wrap that is in progress, clearing the wrap-in-progress state so a fresh prepare_wrap can run. Call this when prepare_wrap refuses with 'a wrap is already in progress' and that wrap is NOT going to be finished — typically one an earlier session opened and then ended without saving, so nothing is left to compress it. Episodes are NOT deleted: cancelling discards the frozen snapshot and its handshake token, and every episode in the abandoned window is still recorded and is picked up by the next prepare_wrap. The cancellation is written to the audit trail with the abandoned token and episode IDs. Check who owns the wrap before cancelling it. One server process runs per client session against a shared store, so the wrap may belong to another session that is still running and part-way through composing its compression; cancelling makes that session's save fail and throws its work away. Call `status` first — it reports when the wrap started, and one opened moments ago is probably a live peer rather than a corpse. Prefer finishing a wrap you opened yourself. Do not call this to recover from a save_continuity validation failure you can fix by editing the text and saving again — that wrap is still live and cancelling it throws away the snapshot you are working against. If you opened the wrap yourself, pass the wrap_token prepare_wrap gave you: the cancel then succeeds only if that wrap is still the one in progress, and is refused without changing anything if a peer replaced it. Omit wrap_token to cancel whatever is current, which is what you want when recovering a wrap you did not open. Exception: a wrap prepared under the consolidate gate is cancelled without its token only when session_id is the session that prepared it, or with force=true when that session is gone; a wrap opened with a token its preparer supplied is cancelled without that token only with force=true. PARTIAL (corrupt) wrap state is cleared with partial=true, which refuses if a healthy wrap has replaced it.

force.description: Cancel a gated wrap without its token or session, or a wrap opened with a caller-supplied token without that token, when its preparer is gone. Discards its compression.

partial.description: Clear PARTIAL (corrupt, unsaveable) wrap state, and only that: refused with no change if a healthy wrap is in progress or the store is idle. Needs no token. Cannot be combined with wrap_token.

session_id.description: Your session. Without wrap_token, a wrap prepared under the consolidate gate is cancelled only when this is the session that prepared it.

wrap_token.description: Optional proof that the wrap being cancelled is yours — the token prepare_wrap returned. The store compares it inside the same transaction that clears, so a peer cannot swap the wrap in between. Refused with no change if it does not match, including when the wrap has already completed. Omit it to cancel whatever is in progress (a gated wrap also needs session_id or force; a wrap opened with a caller-supplied token needs force).

value.name: wrap_cancel

value.description: Delete a single episode by ID. Use this for content that should not exist: accidentally recorded PII, sensitive data, or fundamentally wrong recordings. Do NOT use for factual corrections — record a new episode with the correction instead and let compression resolve it. The deletion is logged in the audit trail. The text is removed from the episodes table and overwritten in the database file (secure_delete); the WAL is emptied after the delete, or at the store's next delete or close if another connection is reading at that moment. By default, a tombstone is preserved as an existence proof for audit integrity: episode ID, original timestamp, episode type, and a content hash keyed by a per-store salt; a new episode's id is keyed by it too. The salt is kept in the database, never in the audit trail, so a guess at deleted content cannot be checked against the audit trail alone; whoever holds the database file can still guess short content from the tombstone. Disable tombstones at Store construction (keep_tombstones=False) if no hash should stay in the database. Episodes recorded before the store was upgraded, and team-imported episodes, carry an unsalted hash and id, which can be guessed for short content. The audit trail keeps each event's source, time and type in clear. Not reached: backups, the migration's .bak copy, other copies of the file, and text already consolidated into the memory file. The hash chain remains verifiable either way. This action is irreversible.

episode_id.description: The 8-character hex ID of the episode to delete. Use recall or prepare_wrap to find episode IDs.

value.name: delete_episode

value.description: Get memory health metrics. Call this at session start to understand memory state, or when diagnosing issues. Returns episode counts (total and since last wrap), wrap history, continuity file size, episodes by type, whether a wrap is currently in progress, and audit trail health (enabled/disabled, entry count, log path, retention window). Use `anneal-memory verify` from the CLI to validate the audit hash chain itself — status() only surfaces cheap health signals, not integrity proof.

value.description: Plant a spore — an open cognitive loop in the PROSPECTIVE layer (a thing that must RESOLVE), distinct from episodic/continuity memory (which accretes and never completes). Use for an open intention you want to carry forward and close later: a `task` (open doing), a `question` (open not-knowing), or a `thought` (open idea). Set `tier` to weight intent (hot/warm/cold/parked) and `next` (YYYY-MM-DD or YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM) to ask for re-surfacing on a date. Resolve later via spore_descend (compost) or spore_ascend (transmute into memory/a project).

episode_id.description: The 8-character hex ID of the episode to delete. Use recall or prepare_wrap to find episode IDs.

domain.description: Optional free-text domain tag (e.g. health, strategic, flow).

next.description: YYYY-MM-DD or YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM (local time) — when to re-surface (a reminder date, NOT a deadline).

pointer.description: Optional link to fuller context for the loop as it stands.

type.description: What KIND of openness: task=doing, question=not-knowing, thought=idea.

kind.description: Terminal kind; must be valid for the intention's type.

intention_id.description: Intention id, e.g. 'intention-007' (an older 'spore-007' reads too).

kind.description: Promote target; must be valid for the intention's type.

ref.description: What the intention became (project path / episode id / pattern name).

top_of_mind.description: Only the hot-or-growing ToM contribution (default false = all open).

next.description: YYYY-MM-DD or YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM, or empty string to clear.

max_chars.description: Hard limit on the memory file in characters: the prompt states it and save_continuity enforces it. Default 26000.

tz.description: IANA time zone a day is cut in, e.g. 'America/New_York'. Default: the server machine's own.

include_superseded.description: Also return episodes a newer episode replaced, marked with what replaced them. Default false: they are left out.

keyword.description: Search episode content for this keyword or phrase. An exact phrase match is tried first; a multi-word phrase with no exact match is then matched word by word and ranked.

limit.description: Maximum episodes to return. Default for a keyword recall ranked by relevance: up to 20, stopping before about 24,000 characters; 100 otherwise. When a multi-word keyword has no exact match and is ranked word by word, the default is 10 instead; pass a limit to see more.

offset.description: Skip first N matching episodes. Default 0.

order.description: relevance: episodes most about the keyword first (how often it occurs for the episode's length, and whether in its opening), newest first among equals; the default when a keyword is given. newest: by timestamp, newest first; the default without a keyword. Both list the same matches.

since.description: ISO 8601 timestamp — return episodes after this time.

until.description: ISO 8601 timestamp — return episodes before this time.

content.description: The episode content — what happened, what was observed, decided, or questioned.

derived_from.description: Ids of the episodes this content was derived from, e.g. your summary of a page you recorded as external. Each must exist. It then counts at most as trusted as its most trusted source, so a summary of an external page reads as external.

episode_type.description: Episode type. observation=pattern/insight, decision=committed choice, tension=conflict/tradeoff, question=open question, outcome=result of action, context=environmental/state info.

metadata.description: Optional JSON metadata to attach to the episode.

source.description: Agent or source attribution. Defaults to 'agent'.

state_key.description: The state slot this fact fills, e.g. 'user.home_city'. A newer episode with the same key replaces this one, and this one replaces older episodes with the key, with no word-overlap check: the shared key is your claim that the facts fill one slot. recall then hides the older episode and, for a keyword that matches it, names this one as its replacement. Case and spacing are ignored.

supersedes.description: Ids of older episodes this one replaces (a changed fact). Each must exist, not be newer, and share at least a quarter of the shorter text's meaningful words with this content; otherwise nothing is recorded. recall then hides the old episode by default.

trust.description: Where the content came from. agent (default) = your own observation or decision; tool = a tool result you are relaying; external = a web page, document or another party. Recall marks tool/external content as data, not instruction. Use tool/external whenever the content is someone else's claim.

max_chars.description: Leave it out: the save uses the limit the step was prepared with. A value is accepted only if it equals that limit.

wrap_token.description: Required. The 32-char hex token from the prepare_wrap reply (the 'Wrap token: <hex>' line). It says which step this reply answers: without it, or with a stale or wrong one, nothing is saved.

domain.description: Optional free-text domain tag (e.g. health, strategic, flow).

next.description: YYYY-MM-DD or YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM (local time) — when to re-surface (a reminder date, NOT a deadline).

pointer.description: Optional link to fuller context for the loop as it stands.

type.description: What KIND of openness: task=doing, question=not-knowing, thought=idea.

kind.description: Transmute target; must be valid for the spore's type.

ref.description: What the spore became (project path / episode id / pattern name).

kind.description: Terminal kind; must be valid for the spore's type.

top_of_mind.description: Only the hot-or-growing ToM contribution (default false = all open).

next.description: YYYY-MM-DD or YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM, or empty string to clear.

force.description: Cancel a gated wrap without its token or session, or a wrap opened with a caller-supplied token without that token, when its preparer is gone. Discards its compression.

partial.description: Clear PARTIAL (corrupt, unsaveable) wrap state, and only that: refused with no change if a healthy wrap is in progress or the store is idle. Needs no token. Cannot be combined with wrap_token.

session_id.description: Your session. Without wrap_token, a wrap prepared under the consolidate gate is cancelled only when this is the session that prepared it.

wrap_token.description: Optional proof that the wrap being cancelled is yours — the token prepare_wrap returned. The store compares it inside the same transaction that clears, so a peer cannot swap the wrap in between. Refused with no change if it does not match, including when the wrap has already completed. Omit it to cancel whatever is in progress (a gated wrap also needs session_id or force; a wrap opened with a caller-supplied token needs force).
